MAIRO VERGARA  
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
Transcript | Lesson 06 
Hi, I’m Sonja Burger.  The three phrasal verbs that we will focus on today are 
keep on, make up and back up.  We’ll start with keep on and we’ll look at the 
three meanings on which we will focus today.  I am going to read them to 
you and then I will show you a slide, which I’d like you to read yourself.  So 
you will hear the meanings and then you will see them and then we’ll 
proceed to look at the sample sentences.  
The first meaning of keep on is to continue doing something or to do 
something repeatedly.  The second meaning is to continue employing 
someone and the third meaning is to talk continuously about something or 
to repeat yourself so many times that it becomes annoying.  
Now I’d like you to read these three meanings on a slide and then once 
you’ve finished reading them, we’ll start looking at sample sentences.  
So let’s start with the first meaning of ‘keep on’: To continue doing 
something or to do something many times. Sample sentence:  
Keep on practicing and before you know it, you’ll be a soccer star. 
Now let’s analyze the phrasal verb ‘keep on’.  ‘Keep’ is a verb that means ‘to 
maintain a certain state or effort’ and ‘on’ suggests a forward motion or 
movement.  There’s a lot of psychology in the phrasal verb ‘keep on’ because 
on the one hand it suggests sustained effort and on the other hand it 
suggests forward motion and therefore a person who manages to sustain a 
certain effort, who manages to keep practicing for instance and manages to 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
look forward to success is a motivated person.  So ‘keep on’ doing what 
you’re doing and you will taste success.   
The second meaning is to keep employing someone.  Let’s look at a sample 
sentence:  
Why do you keep this guy on despite his bad attitude?   
So this guy thinks he’s God’s gift to the workplace.  He’s arrogant, he thinks 
he knows better than everyone else and he has shockingly bad relationships 
with his colleagues, yet the boss keeps him on.  Let’s find out why.   
Excuse me sir, why do you keep this guy on if he has such a bad attitude? 
 The boss answers, “Because he’s a technical genius.  There isn’t a computer 
he cannot fix.” So there you have the reason.  
The third meaning is to say something repeatedly to the point where it 
annoys other people.  Sample sentence:  
My mother-in-law keeps on and on about how lucky I am to have married 
her son.   
So it’s clear from this sentence that the mother-in-law is not very happy 
with her daughter-in-law and I think the feeling is mutual.  And the 
daughter-in-law’s irritation is seen in that repetition; ‘keep on and on’.  
The second phrasal verb we will discuss today is the phrasal verb ‘make up’ 
and incredibly, this phrasal verb has more than 8 meanings. But today we 
are going to look at 8 meanings, and first of all, I would like you to read 
these meanings on two separate slides.  Read them with attention and take 
in what you read and then after you’ve read the slides, I will go through each 
meaning separately.  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
The first meaning of ‘make up’ is to invent a story, to make up a story.  And 
a perfect example would be CS Lewis, the well-known writer of ‘The 
Chronicles of Narnia’.  You might have read the books or you might have 
seen the movies.  Now when CS Lewis was young, he and his brother Warren 
made up, they invented a whole country and then they carried on and 
invented a 400-year history for that country.  They made up a 400-year 
history.  Now that is amazing.  
The second meaning is to improvise. A good example sentence would be:  
I don’t have a specific itinerary for my world trip.  I’ll make it up as I go.  
Whatever moves me!’  Now, we don’t know where this guy is going to be in a 
week’s time.  He is going to make it up.  He is going to improvise. He might 
be in Guarujá, in Guangzhou, in Glasgow or maybe in Grand Rapids. 
Whatever moves him.  
The third meaning of ‘make up’ is to compensate for. To ‘make up’ for 
something that you had done wrong.  A good sample sentence would be: In 
the last few months of his life, the cancer patient tried to make up for all 
the broken relationships in his life. 
Now doctors will tell you, doctors who work with terminal patients that is, 
that is patients who are dying, they will tell you that restoring relationships, 
reconciling with your loved ones, is tremendously comforting when you are 
dying.  So in this case, the cancer patient made up for broken relationships.  
And now the next meaning, and I am sure all of you know this meaning and 
that is to make up your face.  To put cosmetics on your face.  A good sample 
sentence would be:  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
4 
When you apply a pencil to your brows, always apply the line at the top 
of the brow because gives the illusion of lift.  
And the fifth meaning ‘to decide’, ‘to make up your mind’ is usually the 
phrase that we use.   
I have made up my mind. You will not go into a flat next year.  I expect 
you to stay in res,  t’s cheaper and it is safer. 
So this father doesn’t want his daughter to move out into a flat to live by 
herself.  He thinks it is too expensive and it might not be safe.  He has made 
up his mind about the correct course of action.  
And the sixth meaning:  To ‘make up’ after a quarrel. To reconcile. Now, to 
reconcile means to restore relationships between people. So the best part of 
a quarrel is making up afterwards. I don’t have to go into the details there.  
The seventh meaning of ‘make up’ is ‘to consist of’.  A sample sentence 
would be:  
The rescue team is made up of a doctor, a tracker and a mountaineer. 
Now here, there’s a sense of a whole consisting of parts.  In this case, of 
three different people.  The party, the rescue party, is made up of three 
people.  
And then the eighth meaning refers to the world of printing and publishing.  
We have to make up the pages before they can go to the printers.  
So before you send the magazine or newspaper pages to the printers, you 
have to check the layout or do the layout.  You have to make sure that the 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
5 
editing is done properly and you also have to make sure that the whole look 
of the page is right and then you can send it to the printers.  
And that is ‘make up’ for you; Eight different meanings.  
The third and last phrasal verb that we’re going to discuss today is ‘back up’. 
Now, we’re going to look at 6 different meanings and once again, I would 
like you to read those meanings on 2 slides. Read them with attention, as I 
have said before and after that, I will go through the meanings with you.  
Let’s start with the first meaning of the phrasal verb, ‘back up’: ‘to make a 
copy of’. And here is the sample sentence:  
I have no sympathy for you. I told you to make a backup your doctoral 
thesis and you were too lazy to do it and now you’ve lost three months’ 
work. 
So yes, this guy has worked very hard but one tends to lose a bit of sympathy 
for him because he had been warned. He should have known better.  He did 
not make a copy.  And he didn’t store it safely in another place so he has lost 
his work because he didn’t back it up.  
Number 2: ‘to support’.  And here I’d like to use an example from the pub. 
Excuse the bit of acting.  
Hey, buddy, are you going to support, are you going to back up my story 
to my wife that we did not, I repeat, we did not go past the pub? 
Yes, this guy wants his friend to back up his lie, it’s not a story, it’s a lie, and 
to convince his wife that they haven’t had a pint or two too many.  But I’m 
inclined to think she’s not going to believe either of them.  
Number 3: ‘to prove that something is right’.  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
6 
The best argumentative essays are essays in which arguments are 
backed up by sound research.  
So in this case, you back up. You prove your arguments by providing good 
statistics and good research.  
The fourth meaning of ‘back up’ is ‘pile up’ as in cars. And here’s a sample 
sentence for you:  
The highway was backed up for miles and miles after two furniture 
removal trucks had collided. Lounge suites, mattresses and dining room 
suits were strewn all over the road. 
Now, I’m sure you can see this in your mind’s eye.  All those impatient 
drivers in their backed up cars drumming their fingers on the steering wheel. 
Yes, all because the highway is backed up.  
Now number 5 is to make a person or thing go backwards and here I want 
you to imagine a jam packed lift. Everyone has trollies laden with summer 
sale bargains and they all want to get out of the lift.  You can’t wait to get 
out of this smelly lift with that human smell.  And when the doors open, you 
have this stampede of angry shoppers all wanting to get in and you caught 
halfway between the lift and the stampede of angry cows, I mean people, and 
that’s when you say  
Could you please back up a bit. 
In other words, go backwards.  
The final meaning, meaning number 6 is to block. And here I’d like to read 
the last sample sentence to you.  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
7 
The main water supply was backed up, leaving the whole neighborhood 
without water for an hour. 
So when a pipe is backed up it’s blocked and water can’t flow through, the 
thing you don’t want is a backed up toilet.  
And that is the end of today’s lesson.  The moral of the story, keep on living.  
There’s no recipe to make it up as you go along.  And finally, remember; 
always back up your computer files.

Hi, this is Melissa Faulkner, coming to you from Durham, North Carolina.  
Today we are going to talk about three phrasal verbs - ‘fall apart’, ‘put up 
with’ and ‘pass out’.  Now for each phrasal verb, I’m going to give you 
three sentences.  We’ll talk about how to use those three phrasal verbs in a 
sentence, with a short explanation.   
So let’s go ahead and get started with the first phrasal verb.  ‘Fall apart’. 
Now, ‘fall apart’ has two kind of different meanings, one of them is literal 
and one of them is figurative.  So the first version of ‘fall apart’ is a 
material.  Sort of when a material starts to break up or disintegrate, when 
it starts to come apart, we would say that it’s falling apart.  Now the more 
figurative version of this verbal phrase ‘fall apart’ is when sort of an idea 
or a plan starts to fall apart.  It starts to become disorganized or it starts 
to go differently than you expected it to go.  
So let’s get started with sentence number one: 
The bread on the sandwich was soaked with mayonnaise and it soon 
began to fall apart.   
So in this case, to ‘fall apart’ means that a material or something physical 
is falling apart.  So in this case, there is mayonnaise on the sandwich, so 
mayonnaise is a sauce.  The sauce is making the bread sort of soft and it’s 
causing the bread to fall apart, to come apart or to break. So when you are 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
eating the sandwich, sort of its soaked in sauce, and it becomes very 
difficult to eat because the bread is sort of coming apart.  
Let’s move on to sentence number two:  
After the visiting team scored 10 runs in the seventh inning, the home 
team began to fall apart.   
Now, this is that second version of the phrase ‘fall apart’.  It is the more 
figurative version of ‘fall apart’. So this means that the team was 
becoming disorganized or ineffective. So when the visiting team came, 
they scored 10 points, they scored 10 runs in the seventh inning and the 
home team started to get discouraged.  They maybe didn’t catch the ball as 
well; they weren’t hitting as well.  They were falling apart or becoming 
disorganized as a team.  
Let’s move on to sentence number 3: 
Jeff’s old wooden fishing boat had been in the family for over 30 years 
and the water damage was causing it to fall apart.   
So in this case, ‘fall apart’ means to break apart or to disintegrate.  So you 
can imagine that this boat has been around for 30 years. It’s probably 
been on a dock somewhere, in the water for all that time.  The water is 
starting to make the wood come apart or break apart so the fishing boat is 
starting to fall apart.  It’s not as good as it once was.  
Let’s move on to the second phrasal verb ‘put up with’. Now ‘put up with’ 
means when there is a situation that’s sort of unpleasant or not a great 
situation, but even though it’s not a great situation, you are patient and 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
you decide to accept that situation as best you can, so you ‘put up with’ 
the situation.  
So let’s go on to sentence number 1:  
Alison couldn’t put up with her boss’ mean comments about her 
weight any longer. 
So in this case, Alison has a boss. He has maybe been making some mean 
comments about her weight, maybe how she needs to lose some weight 
and she’s been patient for a really long time because it’s her boss and she 
doesn’t want to lose her job. But at this point, he’s been giving these mean 
comments for such a long time that she’s just getting tired of it.  She just 
can’t put up with it anymore.  Maybe she’s going to say something to him, 
maybe she is even going to quit, but she can’t put up with it anymore.  
Let’s go on to sentence number 2:  
Caleb has to put up with how slow his computer is because he doesn’t 
want to spend money on a new one right now. 
 So in this situation, Caleb’s computer is really slow.  Maybe he’s trying to 
write a document or do some work on his computer and it’s taking forever 
to load or to save and it’s really annoying. But he doesn’t want to buy a 
new computer right now.  He doesn’t want to spend any money.  So, he is 
patient with his computer.  He decides to put up with the fact that his 
computer is so slow so that he doesn’t have to buy a new one.  
Sentence number3:

4 
Even though Jaylin is a procrastinator, Mr. Jones puts up with it 
because Jaylin always turns in excellent writing. 
Now in this situation, Jaylin is a procrastinator.  A procrastinator is 
someone who doesn’t turn in their work on time or waits until the very 
last minute to turn their work in. So Mr. Jones normally would punish 
Jaylin because he’s either turning his work in late or he’s turning it in 
right at the last minute.  But Mr. Jones decides to put up with it, he 
decides to be patient with Jaylin because every time Jaylin does turn in 
his work, it’s really awesome, it is excellent work, so he decides to put up 
with it.  He’s patient with Jaylin.  
Let’s move on to our third phrasal verb - ‘pass out’.  Now there are two 
different versions of the phrase ‘pass out’.  The first version means when 
you’re passing something out, it means that you’re giving out multiple 
items.  So maybe there’s a group and you are giving out things to the 
group. Maybe you have a lot of items and you’re giving them out or you’re 
passing them out.  The second version, ‘to pass out’ means to faint or to 
fall down.  So when someone has a medical condition, maybe they’re 
feeling lightheaded or they’re feeling a little sick and they sort of go 
unconscious for a second and fall down to the ground, we would call that 
passing out.  
So let’s start with sentence number 1:  
Mrs. Rose wanted to pass out lollipops to her students but they were 
being extremely disrespectful, so she kept them in her bag.

In this case, Mrs. Rose is probably a teacher.  She has a group of students.

being a little disrespectful so she decides not to.  But she would have 
originally passed out or given out her lollipops to her students.

were passing out 100 coupons for a free refrigerator. 
So in this case, Walmart is having a sale.  They have 100 coupons and the 
first 100 people to come, get a coupon for a free refrigerator.  So in this 
case, the buyer, the person in the sentence, is going to get up really early 
to make sure that they are in line to be one of the first 100 people because 
Walmart is passing out coupons and so they want to get one of those 
coupons to get a free refrigerator.  
Let’s take a look at sentence number 3:   
When Laura saw the stitches on the bottom of Jacob’s foot, she felt 
sick to her stomach and then she eventually passed out. 
So this is that second version of the phrase ‘pass out’.  It means to 
medically go unconscious.  So Laura looked at Jacob’s foot, it had stitches 
on it, maybe it looked really gross.  Laura doesn’t like looking at gross 
things and so her stomach starts to feel bad and then eventually she 
passes out.  She goes unconscious.  She falls to the ground.  Somebody has 
to help wake her up or they have to call the ER or something like that.  So 
she passed out.  She fell to the ground.

and ‘pass out’.  I hope these explanations were helpful to you and I hope I

Thanks.

Transcript | Lesson 08 
Hi, my name is Holden Harris and I am from Louisiana in the United States 
and today I’m going to talk to you about three more Phrasal verbs - run out 
of, run out and talk over. 
So the first I want to talk to you about is ‘run out of’ and don’t get confused 
with this phrasal verb because you can say things like ‘I ran out of the house’ 
or ‘I ran out of the store’ and while that’s using a verb and using ‘run out of’ 
that’s not necessarily a phrasal verb. So the phrasal verb examples that I’m 
going to talk to you about come with the definition ‘to use up or finish a 
supply of something’. Okay, so I could say, for example:  
I won’t be able to pay my bills if I run out of money this month.  
In this situation, my money supply is being exhausted and I may not be able 
to pay for my living expenses. So you can run out of money.  
I could also say:  
My mobile phone will run out of power if I don’t charge it.  
In this example, my cell phone battery is being drained and I will, it will soon 
power down if I don’t plug it in. So your battery, you can run out of battery, 
your car can run out of battery, your cell phone, your laptop. Those kinds of 
things. So, basically, you’re using up that battery, you’re exhausting the 
supply of something. 
The last example of ‘run out of’ I have for you is: 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
Ginny was unable to finish her English test because she ran out of time.  
Okay? So time is another thing that you can easily run out of. And in this 
example, Ginny took a test that allowed for a limited amount of time and 
was unable to answer all of her questions. So, maybe she’s taking this test 
and she has 60 minutes to take it, 30 minutes, if she runs out of time she 
can’t complete all of her questions. So, you can run out of a lot of things. 
And like I said, the definition for this is to use up or finish a supply of 
something so think of anything that you can run out of. Maybe you run out 
of food, you run out of time, you run out of battery – I don’t know – there 
are a lot of things that you can run out of.  
Now the next one that I want to talk about is ‘run out’ and similarly ‘run out’ 
can be used to talk about the direction or you leaving a certain place like “we 
were in the house and I ran out.” 
So that means that I ran out of the house but that’s not exactly a phrasal 
verb. So, there are a few definitions, a couple of definitions I have for you for 
‘run out’ and the first example that I want to give you is: 
My apartment lease agreement ran out so I had to move to a new place.  
In this example, contracts only last for a certain amount of time. In this 
case, I have to move out of my apartment because my contract has expired. 
So this definition is to expire or become invalid. Anything that can expire or 
just like I guess the definition says, become invalid can be something that 
runs out. So in this case it’s a lease agreement if you live in an apartment.  
Here’s another example though using that definition: 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
The singer switched to a better record label because her previous label 
contract had run out.  
So in this example, a group of people, you know, basically this singer has a 
contract that runs out because her record label does not permit it to keep 
going on. So yeah, you know, any kind of contract that you make can run 
out, can expire, for example too, my driver’s license. The time on my driver’s 
license ran out. You know, so I don’t have that anymore. 
Okay, another example though, another definition for ‘run out’ is to scare 
away or force someone or something to leave. So you can use this to talk 
about many things and the example I have for you here is:  
Last night, a raccoon was eating from Steve’s prized garden so he ran it 
out.  
Okay? So imagine Steve has a garden and raccoons are trying to steal all his 
food and he says ‘hey!’ you know ‘Don’t eat my food!’ you know? Blah, blah, 
blah… goes, tries to scare away this raccoon.  
So there are a lot of things you can run out. Personally, in my house we have 
some bugs that we try to run out. A couple of years ago we had mice in our 
house that we tried to run out. So any kind of animal or even a person I 
could say that, you know, my mom ran me out of the kitchen because I was 
eating all the cookies or something like that. So when you trying to scare 
away someone, make them move, get out of your way – you’re running them 
out.  
Okay and the last phrasal verb that I want to talk about is ‘talk over’. So ‘talk 
over’ can be used in many ways. And today I’m going to tell you about three 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
4 
of them. So the first ‘talk over’ can mean to discuss something. If you’re 
talking about anything. So the example I have is:  
I’m not sure where I want to go on vacation next year. Let’s sit down and 
talk this over.  
So in this situation, I’m having a dilemma about where I want to go on 
vacation. I’m hoping to sit down and discuss this with someone so that I can 
consider all my options and make a decision. So maybe me and my wife are 
trying to go somewhere and we’re not sure exactly where. Maybe Europe, 
maybe Asia, maybe Australia. But we don’t know and I don’t know, but we 
got to sit down and kind of discuss the situation. We have to figure out how 
much money we have, we have to figure out the kinds of things we want to 
do, the country we want to visit. We have to talk that over. So any time 
you’re going to sit down with someone and discuss something, you’re talking 
it over.  
Now you can also use ‘talk over’ to talk about persuading someone. You can 
talk someone over to your side, per se. And the example I have for you: 
At first, my father wouldn’t let me go camping but I talked him over to 
my side.   
So in this case, I want to go camping but my father will not allow me. So 
after doing my best to persuade him, he finally lets me go. So if you’re able 
to persuade someone to do something - you’re talking them over. So, you 
know, I wanted to buy a dog. My wife didn’t want one but I talked her over. 
So it means that I basically made her agree with me, I persuaded her to agree 
with my decision to get a new dog.  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
5 
And the last definition I have for ‘talk over’ is to speak and be heard amid 
some loud noise. So if there’s something, someone’s playing some loud 
music or your dogs are barking or something is just really, really loud, you 
have to raise your volume and talk over that other noise. So the most basic 
example for this is: 
The teacher had to talk over the noisy students. 
You see this very often when you have a teacher that has a classroom where 
students who are really, really, really loud and they have to teach and they 
talk at this level, then they talk at this level, then they talk at this level. So 
they’re having to talk over the students. You know, they have to talk over 
their volume.  
Alright, so those are three phrasal verbs as I said ‘run out of’, ‘run out’ and 
‘talk over’ and three examples for each of how you can use them. So thank 
you for watching today and I hope you were able to learn something and I 
will see you next time.

pairs.en: So this definition is to expire or become invalid. Anything that can expire or
pairs.pt: just like I guess the definition says, become invalid can be something that

pairs.en: runs out. So in this case it’s a lease agreement if you live in an apartment.
pairs.pt: Here’s another example though using that definition:

pairs.en: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE
pairs.pt: The singer switched to a better record label because her previous label

pairs.en: contract had run out.
pairs.pt: So in this example, a group of people, you know, basically this singer has a

pairs.en: contract that runs out because her record label does not permit it to keep
pairs.pt: going on. So yeah, you know, any kind of contract that you make can run

pairs.en: out, can expire, for example too, my driver’s license. The time on my driver’s
pairs.pt: license ran out. You know, so I don’t have that anymore.

pairs.en: Okay, another example though, another definition for ‘run out’ is to scare
pairs.pt: away or force someone or something to leave. So you can use this to talk

pairs.en: about many things and the example I have for you here is:
pairs.pt: Last night, a raccoon was eating from Steve’s prized garden so he ran it

pairs.en: out.
pairs.pt: Okay? So imagine Steve has a garden and raccoons are trying to steal all his

pairs.en: food and he says ‘hey!’ you know ‘Don’t eat my food!’ you know? Blah, blah,
pairs.pt: blah… goes, tries to scare away this raccoon.

pairs.en: So there are a lot of things you can run out. Personally, in my house we have
pairs.pt: some bugs that we try to run out. A couple of years ago we had mice in our

pairs.en: house that we tried to run out. So any kind of animal or even a person I
pairs.pt: could say that, you know, my mom ran me out of the kitchen because I was

pairs.en: eating all the cookies or something like that. So when you trying to scare
pairs.pt: away someone, make them move, get out of your way – you’re running them

pairs.en: out.
pairs.pt: Okay and the last phrasal verb that I want to talk about is ‘talk over’. So ‘talk

pairs.en: over’ can be used in many ways. And today I’m going to tell you about three
pairs.pt: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

pairs.en: of them. So the first ‘talk over’ can mean to discuss something. If you’re
pairs.pt: talking about anything. So the example I have is:

pairs.en: I’m not sure where I want to go on vacation next year. Let’s sit down and
pairs.pt: talk this over.

pairs.en: So in this situation, I’m having a dilemma about where I want to go on
pairs.pt: vacation. I’m hoping to sit down and discuss this with someone so that I can

pairs.en: consider all my options and make a decision. So maybe me and my wife are
pairs.pt: trying to go somewhere and we’re not sure exactly where. Maybe Europe,

pairs.en: maybe Asia, maybe Australia. But we don’t know and I don’t know, but we
pairs.pt: got to sit down and kind of discuss the situation. We have to figure out how

pairs.en: much money we have, we have to figure out the kinds of things we want to
pairs.pt: do, the country we want to visit. We have to talk that over. So any time

pairs.en: you’re going to sit down with someone and discuss something, you’re talking
pairs.pt: it over.

pairs.en: Now you can also use ‘talk over’ to talk about persuading someone. You can
pairs.pt: talk someone over to your side, per se. And the example I have for you:

pairs.en: At first, my father wouldn’t let me go camping but I talked him over to
pairs.pt: my side.

pairs.en: So in this case, I want to go camping but my father will not allow me. So
pairs.pt: after doing my best to persuade him, he finally lets me go. So if you’re able

pairs.en: to persuade someone to do something - you’re talking them over. So, you
pairs.pt: know, I wanted to buy a dog. My wife didn’t want one but I talked her over.

pairs.en: So it means that I basically made her agree with me, I persuaded her to agree
pairs.pt: with my decision to get a new dog.

pairs.en: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE
pairs.pt: And the last definition I have for ‘talk over’ is to speak and be heard amid

pairs.en: some loud noise. So if there’s something, someone’s playing some loud
pairs.pt: music or your dogs are barking or something is just really, really loud, you

pairs.en: have to raise your volume and talk over that other noise. So the most basic
pairs.pt: example for this is:

pairs.en: The teacher had to talk over the noisy students.
pairs.pt: You see this very often when you have a teacher that has a classroom where

pairs.en: students who are really, really, really loud and they have to teach and they
pairs.pt: talk at this level, then they talk at this level, then they talk at this level. So

pairs.en: they’re having to talk over the students. You know, they have to talk over
pairs.pt: their volume.

pairs.en: Alright, so those are three phrasal verbs as I said ‘run out of’, ‘run out’ and
pairs.pt: ‘talk over’ and three examples for each of how you can use them. So thank

pairs.en: you for watching today and I hope you were able to learn something and I
pairs.pt: will see you next time.

MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
1 
MAIRO VERGARA  
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
Sentences for Anki | Lesson 09 
Front: 
My Aunt Sherry spent three months planning her wedding, but called it off at the last minute 
because she got cold feet. 
Back:  
Call off = to cancel or decide that something in the future will not happen  
When someone decides not to go through with the wedding because they're having doubts, we call it 
getting cold feet. Sherry canceled the wedding because at the last minute she was having serious 
doubts about getting married. 
Front: 
If we get the thunderstorms tonight that the National Weather Service is predicting, we will 
have to call off the baseball game. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or decide that something in the future will not happen  
Baseball is a very popular sport in the United States, but it is a game that can't be played while it is 
raining or if there is thunder or lightning in the vicinity. It is very common for baseball games to be 
canceled because of inclement weather. 
Front: 
We had to call off our fishing trip down on the Gulf Coast because a hurricane was threatening 
the coastline that weekend. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or decide that something in the future will not happen  
Hurricanes are not an uncommon occurrence along the Gulf Coast of the United States. Obviously a 
fishing trip cannot occur when a hurricane is in progress, so in this instance the fishing trip had to be 
canceled. 
Front: 
When the dictator realized that the voters were against him, he decided to call off the 
elections. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or decide that something in the future will not happen  

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
In this instance this despot is going to thwart the will of the people by not allowing elections to 
happen.  
Front: 
I would hate to have to call off my trip for lack of funds, because I have spent so much time 
dreaming about it and planning for it. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or decide that something in the future will not happen  
To be lacking for funds means to not have enough money. It's always a bummer to have to cancel a 
trip that you have been contemplating for so long because you can't afford it. 
Front: 
There were so many bomb threats being called into the soccer stadium that they decided to 
call off the match in the middle of the game for the safety of the fans. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or stop something that is already in progress 
Safe is priority one at any public event. When bomb threats are called in, they have to be taken 
seriously. In this case they decided to cancel the game and send everybody home for the safety of 
everyone involved. 
Front: 
After the ship sunk, they searched the waters extensively for survivors, but had to call off the 
search after a week had passed. 
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or stop something that is already in progress 
Unfortunately, anytime there is a search for survivors or fatalities after an accident, there comes a 
time when the search can no longer continue. When that moment arrives they cancel, or call off the 
search. In this case a week had passed and there was no point in continuing because they had already 
conducted an extensive search. 
Front: 
I had to call off my son's party because too many of his friends were getting drunk and acting 
foolishly.  
Back: 
Call off = to cancel or stop something that is already in progress 
There is no point in continuing a party that has become out-of-control or dangerous. My son's friends 
were out of control and therefore I had to wrap the party up and send everyone home. 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
Front: 
When the mailman entered the yard and the dogs started surrounding him, he yelled at the 
homeowner to call off the dogs. 
Back: 
Call off = to tell an animal or a person or a group to stop attacking someone 
The mailman was feeling threatened and needed the owner of the dogs to intervene so that they 
would no longer continue harassing and terrifying him. So the mailman asked the owner to shout a 
command to his dogs to make them stop barking at and intimidating the mailman. 
Front: 
The military decided to call off the riot police because they didn't want scenes of protesters 
being attacked on the nightly news. 
Back: 
Call off = to tell an animal or a person or a group to stop attacking someone 
Most governments don't want to appear to be repressive. It is never good public relations to have 
common citizens being attacked by armed force, so in this case the government decided to tell the riot 
police to stop using aggressive means to control the protests. 
Front:  
Kids nowadays are so inundated with technology and electronic devices that it often makes it 
really difficult for them not to put off doing their homework. 
Back: 
Put off = to delay doing something, especially because you don't feel like doing it. 
21st-century children are overwhelmed, flooded, and completely surrounded with electronic 
distractions, such as video games and smart phones and computers. These distractions often cause 
them to delay, forget about, and have a hard time doing their homework. 
Front:  
One of the bits of advice my mother always used to give me was "don’t put off until tomorrow 
what you can do today". 
Back: 
Put off = to delay doing something, especially because you don't feel like doing it. 
The advice my mom gave me basically was to not delay or set aside my responsibilities, that it's 
important to get things done right away, and not to be constantly coming up with excuses for 
procrastinating. 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
4 
Front: 
A procrastinator is someone who puts off doing the things that they don't want to do until 
the last minute.  
Back: 
Put off = to delay doing something, especially because you don't feel like doing it. 
A procrastinator is someone who is always thinking of excuses and coming up with reasons why they 
should not do now what they think they will have time to do later. And procrastination generally has 
a negative connotation, because work accomplished at the last minute is rarely the best quality work. 
Front: 
If you continue to put off mastering phrasal verbs, you'll never become truly fluent in English.  
Back: 
Put off = to delay doing something, especially because you don't feel like doing it. 
Phrasal verbs or any other difficult grammar or language task are things that are best confronted 
now, because delaying dealing with them or learning them will just prolong the amount of time it 
takes for us to master a language. 
Front: 
Tom and Sally were planning a wedding for next June, but they had to put it off until the 
following year when they discovered that Tom was being deployed to Afghanistan. 
Back: 
Put off = to change the time or date of something so that it happens later than it was originally 
planned, especially due to a problem or some unforeseen factor  
To be deployed means for somebody who is enlisted in the military to be sent on an overseas mission. 
Tom just found out that he is going to be sent to Afghanistan, so they are going to have to cancel the 
plans they have already made for their June wedding and have to come up with a new date in the 
future. 
Front: 
Renan is going to have to put off his trip to the United States until he can save up more money. 
Back: 
Put off = to change the time or date of something so that it happens later than it was originally 
planned, especially due to a problem or some unforeseen factor  
Traveling is expensive and Renan has realized that he doesn't have enough for his upcoming trip to 
the United States, so he is going to have to make this trip at a later time. 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
5 
Front: 
As a single parent I feel like it's important that I put off dating until I am done raising my kids 
because they need my undivided attention at this point in their life. 
Back:  
Put off = to change the time or date of something so that it happens later than it was originally 
planned, especially due to a problem or some unforeseen factor 
Parents often have to put their needs behind the needs of their kids, so I'm saying that I don't feel 
that dating is appropriate during this period of my life and therefore I'm going to have to wait to do 
it until all the kids have grown up, because they need 100% of my focus. 
Front: 
Many voters are put off by a politician who can't seem to give a direct answer to a simple 
question. 
Back: 
Put off = To make someone not want to do something or to make someone not like something 
or someone 
The inability of a politician to give honest and direct answers is something that upsets, irritates, 
infuriates, and repels voters. This causes voters to lose respect and affection for a politician. 
Front: 
Many girls are put off by guys who come on a little too strong at the beginning. 
Back: 
Put off = To make someone not want to do something or to make someone not like something 
or someone 
If a boy who is interested in a girl and is too aggressive or too forward when he tries to initiate 
conversation with her, it causes many girls to lose interest or even be afraid of this guy. It can 
decrease his chances of convincing her to go out with him. 
Front: 
Honey, I'm really put off by the fact that you have such poor table manners at dinner time 
and you're always burping without covering your mouth or apologizing. 
Back:  
Put off = To make someone not want to do something or to make someone not like something 
or someone 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
6 
This woman is tired of the fact that her husband acts in a gross manner at the dinner table. It causes 
her to feel less attracted to him that he is not polite and that he doesn't hide his bodily functions 
when they are having a meal together. 
Front: 
If you have told somebody that you have forgiven them for a past offense, it's really best never 
to bring it up again in the future. 
Back: 
Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something 
If a bank forgave you a debt, they would no longer send you a bill. Likewise, if you forgive somebody 
for something that they have done to you, if you have truly let go of it, it's not something you should 
ever mention again in the future. 
Front: 
I hate to bring this up, but you still owe me $100! 
Back:  
Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something 
It's often awkward to ask somebody for money, so understandably the person who loaned the money 
may feel uncomfortable about broaching the subject of the $100. 
Front: 
Grandma, next time you visit the doctor, don't forget to bring up all the heartburn you've been 
suffering. 
Back: 
Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something 
In this case the grandmother is being reminded not to forget to mention this chronic problem with 
heartburn she's having at her next routine checkup. 
Front: 
I know that you think employees here don't get enough breaks, so don't forget to bring that 
up when the owner shows up at our next meeting.  
Back: 
Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something 
Workers at any business often have concerns or complaints and it's important for them to remember 
to discuss these issues when they have a chance to speak with the business owner. To show up means 
to make an appearance or arrive somewhere. 
Front: 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
7 
As a father of four I can tell you that bringing up children is not for the faint of heart. 
Back: 
Bring up = to raise or be the primary caregiver for a child 
Someone who is faint of heart is someone who doesn't have the strength of character or the grit to 
handle adversity well. Being a good parent and rearing children requires being able to deal with these 
sometimes challenging situations. 
Front: 
Many people don't realize that Barack Obama spent many years of his childhood 
being brought up by his grandparents.  
Back: 
Bring up = to raise or be the primary caregiver for a child 
President Obama's grandparents played a significant role in taking care of him and raising him when 
he was a minor. 
Front: 
Billy I'm so ashamed of you for robbing that store. That's not how I brought you up!  
Back: 
Bring up = to raise a child with a certain set of morals or standards 
Billy's parents are expressing disappointment. They specifically mention what he did and remind him 
that this crime does not reflect the morals and standards that they tried to inculcate in him. 
Front: 
My parents brought me up to work hard, play by the rules, and show respect to other people. 
Back: 
Bring up = to raise a child with a certain set of morals or standards 
These are the values and the qualities that my parents tried to instill in me when I was younger: 
diligence, respect for the proper way of doing things, and the proper way of treating people. 
Front: 
Kelly would you please go down into the basement and bring up my box full of Christmas 
ornaments? 
Back: 
Bring up = to bring something or someone from a lower place to a higher place 
When we are bringing something from a lower level to a higher level we are bringing it up. If we were 
taking something from an upstairs level down into the basement we would be taking it down into the 
basement. The basement is the lowest level of the house and is generally beneath the ground level. 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
8 
Front: 
Every year I drive to Kansas to pick up my wife's grandmother and bring her up here to Omaha 
to spend Christmas with the family. 
Back:  
Bring up = to bring something or someone from a lower place to a higher place 
Because most maps have north at the top and south at the bottom, many English speakers refer to 
people who live further south as living "down there". So in this sentence, grandmother lives in Kansas 
which is to the south of Omaha. So when she comes to Omaha, she's coming up to Omaha. If we were 
heading from Omaha down to Kansas we would be heading down to Kansas. In short, north is up 
and south is down.

pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: Many girls are put off by guys who come on a little too strong at the beginning.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Put off = To make someone not want to do something or to make someone not like something
pairs.pt: or someone

pairs.en: If a boy who is interested in a girl and is too aggressive or too forward when he tries to initiate
pairs.pt: conversation with her, it causes many girls to lose interest or even be afraid of this guy. It can

pairs.en: decrease his chances of convincing her to go out with him.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: Honey, I'm really put off by the fact that you have such poor table manners at dinner time
pairs.pt: and you're always burping without covering your mouth or apologizing.

pairs.en: Back:
pairs.pt: Put off = To make someone not want to do something or to make someone not like something

pairs.en: or someone
pairs.pt: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

pairs.en: This woman is tired of the fact that her husband acts in a gross manner at the dinner table. It causes
pairs.pt: her to feel less attracted to him that he is not polite and that he doesn't hide his bodily functions

pairs.en: when they are having a meal together.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: If you have told somebody that you have forgiven them for a past offense, it's really best never
pairs.pt: to bring it up again in the future.

pairs.en: Back:
pairs.pt: Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something

pairs.en: If a bank forgave you a debt, they would no longer send you a bill. Likewise, if you forgive somebody
pairs.pt: for something that they have done to you, if you have truly let go of it, it's not something you should

pairs.en: ever mention again in the future.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: I hate to bring this up, but you still owe me $100!
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something
pairs.pt: It's often awkward to ask somebody for money, so understandably the person who loaned the money

pairs.en: may feel uncomfortable about broaching the subject of the $100.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: Grandma, next time you visit the doctor, don't forget to bring up all the heartburn you've been
pairs.pt: suffering.

pairs.en: Back:
pairs.pt: Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something

pairs.en: In this case the grandmother is being reminded not to forget to mention this chronic problem with
pairs.pt: heartburn she's having at her next routine checkup.

pairs.en: Front:
pairs.pt: I know that you think employees here don't get enough breaks, so don't forget to bring that

pairs.en: up when the owner shows up at our next meeting.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to mention something or start a conversation about something
pairs.pt: Workers at any business often have concerns or complaints and it's important for them to remember

pairs.en: to discuss these issues when they have a chance to speak with the business owner. To show up means
pairs.pt: to make an appearance or arrive somewhere.

pairs.en: Front:
pairs.pt: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

pairs.en: As a father of four I can tell you that bringing up children is not for the faint of heart.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to raise or be the primary caregiver for a child
pairs.pt: Someone who is faint of heart is someone who doesn't have the strength of character or the grit to

pairs.en: handle adversity well. Being a good parent and rearing children requires being able to deal with these
pairs.pt: sometimes challenging situations.

pairs.en: Front:
pairs.pt: Many people don't realize that Barack Obama spent many years of his childhood

pairs.en: being brought up by his grandparents.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to raise or be the primary caregiver for a child
pairs.pt: President Obama's grandparents played a significant role in taking care of him and raising him when

pairs.en: he was a minor.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: Billy I'm so ashamed of you for robbing that store. That's not how I brought you up!
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to raise a child with a certain set of morals or standards
pairs.pt: Billy's parents are expressing disappointment. They specifically mention what he did and remind him

pairs.en: that this crime does not reflect the morals and standards that they tried to inculcate in him.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: My parents brought me up to work hard, play by the rules, and show respect to other people.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to raise a child with a certain set of morals or standards
pairs.pt: These are the values and the qualities that my parents tried to instill in me when I was younger:

pairs.en: diligence, respect for the proper way of doing things, and the proper way of treating people.
pairs.pt: Front:

pairs.en: Kelly would you please go down into the basement and bring up my box full of Christmas
pairs.pt: ornaments?

pairs.en: Back:
pairs.pt: Bring up = to bring something or someone from a lower place to a higher place

pairs.en: When we are bringing something from a lower level to a higher level we are bringing it up. If we were
pairs.pt: taking something from an upstairs level down into the basement we would be taking it down into the

pairs.en: basement. The basement is the lowest level of the house and is generally beneath the ground level.
pairs.pt: MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

pairs.en: Front:
pairs.pt: Every year I drive to Kansas to pick up my wife's grandmother and bring her up here to Omaha

pairs.en: to spend Christmas with the family.
pairs.pt: Back:

pairs.en: Bring up = to bring something or someone from a lower place to a higher place
pairs.pt: Because most maps have north at the top and south at the bottom, many English speakers refer to

pairs.en: people who live further south as living "down there". So in this sentence, grandmother lives in Kansas
pairs.pt: which is to the south of Omaha. So when she comes to Omaha, she's coming up to Omaha. If we were

pairs.en: heading from Omaha down to Kansas we would be heading down to Kansas. In short, north is up
pairs.pt: and south is down.

Transcript | Lesson 09 
Hello my friends, this is your, phrasal verbs guru Brooks Gillespie. And 
today, I’m in kind of an interesting location. I’m in Bennington, Nebraska, 
which is a few miles from where I live and it’s a small town and I am by an 
elementary school, which you can probably see in the background and there 
is a baseball diamond. Baseball’s very popular sport in the United States. So, 
I’m outdoors and it’s kind of a chilly day but it’s nice to get out of the 
apartment and just have a, a change of pace. Behind me you can see the 
cloudy skies. So it’s kind of a cloudy day and you can hear the birds singing. 
Anyway, today… I’m apologizing in advance… I have allergies and in 
springtime it’s not uncommon for people in, the United States to do a little 
bit of sniffling… cause, you know, there’s pollen floating around and it’s 
something that people in South America don’t really experience with 
Summer like conditions all year around. But today we’re talking about 3 
phrasal verbs. The verbs are ‘put off’, ‘call off’ and ‘bring up’. And we’re going 
to start with ‘put off’. 
Now I’m come up with 3 sentences and each one has a slightly different 
meaning. The first one it… has to do with delaying something. Especially 
something that you don’t want to do. And the sentence that I came up with 
is a little bit of advice that my Mom used to give me when I was a child, and 
here’s the sentence: 
One of the bits of advice my mother always used to give me was “Don’t 
put off until tomorrow what you can do today”. 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
And that means don’t delay. Don’t wait to do something until a later time. 
To ‘put it off’ means to wait to do it. And my mother always encouraged me 
to do things now. Do your chores now. Do your homework now. Don’t wait 
until tomorrow. If you have time now – get it done. Then you can relax and 
not have to worry about it anymore. The second definition for ‘to put off’ 
has to do with changing, it’s similar but slightly different, changing the time 
or date of something. Especially if you already scheduled it and you need to 
reschedule it for a later time. And the sentence I came up with for that was: 
Tom and Sally were planning a wedding for next June but they had to 
put it off or they had to put off until the following year when they 
discovered that Tom was being deployed to Afghanistan. 
So in this case they had a very big life event – a wedding – scheduled, ready 
to go, but something else happened that they weren’t expecting. The 
husband had to be deployed. Which meant he had to go serve in the military 
overseas so they had to change their plans, they had to put off the wedding. 
They scheduled it for one time, they had to put the wedding off until 
another time.  
And the other definition is to make someone not want to do something or 
not like somebody. So in this case, if you’re – if you are put off by something, 
something makes you not like it so much. And the example here is: 
Many girls are put off by guys who come on a little too strong at the 
beginning.  
So this is a situation where, a guy comes up to a girl in a bar and “hey baby 
how you doing” maybe he’s a little too strong. That might put off the girl. 
She might be like ah I’m put off by his, his forwardness his abrasiveness. So 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
those are three examples of ‘put off’. Our next verb is, or next phrasal verb is 
‘call off’, to ‘call off’. Again, I have three different definitions. The first one is 
to cancel or decide that something won’t happen. So, we’re not delaying 
something, we are cancelling it completely. The first example was this. True 
story:  
My aunt Sherry spent three months planning her wedding but called it 
off at the last minute because she got cold feet. 
To ‘get cold feet’ meant to she started to wonder if she really wanted to do it. 
Cold feed means you’re a little bit hesitant you’re not sure. So she wasn’t 
sure she wanted to marry the guy so she called the wedding off at the last 
minute. The second definition has to do with cancelling something that’s 
already in progress. I think in this case its really appropriate that I’m next to 
a ball diamond. See that’s a baseball diamond. Ah, baseball cannot be played 
in the rain. If I was here and there was a ball game in progress and thunder 
and lightning entered, came across the sky. They would have to call off the 
game. Because it’s unsafe to be out here when the lightening is striking, and 
you really can’t play baseball in the rain it’s not a sport that you can play in 
any sort of weather. Here’s a sample sentence I came up with:  
I had to call off my son’s party because too many of his friends were 
getting drunk and acting foolishly.  
So in this case, again, the party is in progress, it’s happening, the kids are 
here but they’re getting out of control, they’re drinking too much, I’ve lost 
control so I have decided we’re going to call off this party and send 
everybody home. And the last example for call off has to do with telling an 
animal or person to stop attacking. I’m a mailman, that’s what I do. That’s 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
4 
my main job, as a mailman. So I deliver letters and I walk into people’s yards 
and it’s not uncommon to see a dog and if a dog frightens me or threatens 
me I may say ‘Hey, could you call off your dog? Could you call off your dog? 
He’s scaring me’ My actual sentence has to do with that.  
When the mailman entered the yard and the dogs started surrounding 
him, he yelled at the homeowner to call off the dogs.  
So in this case, I’m asking him to yell at the dogs and have them come back. 
Call them off. Call off the dogs please.  
And that brings us to our third and final phrasal verb for the day. And that is 
‘bring up’. Bring up. The first example has to do with, mentioning something 
or starting a conversation about something. That’s what bringing something 
up is.  
Grandma, next time you visit the doctor, don’t forget to bring up all the 
heartburn you’ve been suffering.  
So, I’m telling grandma, don’t forget to mention that. When you’re at the 
doctor don’t forget about the heartburn issues you’re having. Bring that up. 
Remember to bring that up. Remember to mention it or talk about it. 
Second definition for bring up is to raise or be the primary caregiver for a 
child. So if you are raising a child, you are bringing up a child. Many, here’s 
my sentence:  
Many people don’t realize that Barack Obama spent many years being 
brought up by his grandparents.  
If my recollection serves me correctly, his mother was a professional woman 
and she studied and I think she travelled and she couldn’t always be with 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
5 
him. So, his grandparents played a big role in bringing him up. He was 
brought up not only by his mother but he spent a lot of time being brought 
up as well by his grandparents. And our final definition for bring up is 
similar but it has more to do with. Oh I’m sorry, excuse me – this one has to 
do with transporting something from a lower place to a higher place. If you 
can get a look here, I am actually standing on the bleachers here, Kind of a 
bad shot but if somebody was sitting further down and I wanted them to 
bring something to me, I might say ‘hey could you, could you bring that, that 
pop up to me, could you bring that soda up to me’. Because I’m up here and 
they are down here. So to bring something up means to literally and 
physically take an item and transport it from a lower place to a higher place. 
And my sentence in this case was: 
Kelly, would you please go down into the basement and bring up my box 
full of Christmas ornaments.  
So it’s Christmas time, I’m decorating the house, and I’m asking Kelly who, 
let’s just pretend she’s my daughter – ‘Hey Kelly, could you go down and 
bring those up’. In the Midwest, where I live here in Nebraska, most people 
have basements. And one very important reason for that is we are at a high 
risk for tornados. We get big, especially this time a year, right now it’s May 
that I’m filming, in May and June our big, that’s the time of year that we get 
the most thunderstorms. You can see the big clouds in the sky. We got the 
big open sky all around us. Um, and these big storms come across the prairie 
and oftentimes they bring severe winds, hail, and occasionally tornados. 
And, to have a basement is very important because it’s the only place where 
you can be really safe. Sometimes, when these tornados destroy a town, the 
only reason people survive is because they were in the basement. So the 

 
MAIRO VERGARA ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
6 
house gets blown away but that lower level underground is, is a safe place. 
And of course we store things in the basement. And if we want to, we want 
the things in the basement up on a higher level we have to go down there 
and bring them up.  
So that wraps it up for today, it’s a pleasure to chat with all of you once 
again. Happy studying! Have a great evening, or day or morning or whatever 
it is. Tchau!

ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

MAIRO VERGARA  
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
Sentences For Anki | Lesson 10 
FRONT 
 For tomorrow’s lesson find out who sculpted the famous Art Deco sculpture of Jesus Christ, 
called Christ the Redeemer, in Rio de Janeiro. 
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
In this case the teacher is instructing the students to do research (to find out information) in 
preparation for a class.   
FRONT 
You’re all insisting on a family ski trip to Switzerland but has anyone bothered to find out 
how much it will cost us? 
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
In this sentence the fact that the family has not done any research (has not found out the 
price of an expensive overseas holiday) is a problem for the dad. 
FRONT 
I found out by chance who my biological mother was when I visited the dentist’s rooms and 
saw an older version of myself sitting at the switchboard! 
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
In this third sentence information is discovered (found out) by chance, i.e. accidentally. 
BACK 
During my trip to Brazil I found out that Brazilian Portuguese is incredibly musical.  
FRONT 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 

 
 
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
2 
Sometimes learning from experience is as valuable as learning from books. Travel is a great 
tutor!  During his stay in Brazil this young man found out more about the language. He 
learned more about the language of Brazil through experience.  
FRONT 
Read the leaflet to find out what side effects this medication has.  
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
It is important to be informed about the potential side effects of medicine. One way to find 
out what the effects are is to read the leaflet inserted into the packaging of the medication. 
FRONT 
Please find out if the CEO is available for an urgent meeting on Friday. 
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
Many people spend a great deal of their working day looking for information - finding out. 
Information is power. 
FRONT 
If you can find out who authorized the deal, you’ll know who is responsible for the 
fraudulent transactions. 
BACK 
find out = to get information after trying to discover it through study or research or by 
chance 
Sometimes one has to look below the surface to find the information one needs.  
FRONT 
It did not take long before the dishonest secretary was found out. She had been stealing 
from the petty cash box. 
BACK 
find out = to catch in an offense 
We normally use this form of “find out” in its passive voice form - found out. If you are found 
out, someone has discovered that you have done something illegal, dishonest or wrong. This 
secretary was found out because she stole money. 

 
 
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
3 
FRONT 
Believe me, you will be found out! Honesty is the best policy. 
BACK 
find out = to catch in an offense 
People believe they can get away with dishonesty, but one way or another they are found 
out.  
FRONT 
Several very wealthy people who tried to hide money illegally in off-shore entities were 
found out when damning documents were leaked online. 
BACK 
find out = to catch in an offense 
Tax evasion attempts are as old as taxation systems. However, as we have just established 
“honesty is the best policy”. These millionaires and billionaires were left with a lot of egg on 
their faces and many will have to face the music. And there we have covered two idioms in 
addition to covering the phrasal verb “found out”!  The rich people were embarrassed (the 
egg idiom) and many will have to face the consequences (the music idiom) after having been 
found out. Some will be investigated and prosecuted.  
FRONT 
Once Alexander Fleming had figured out that the penicillin mold in one of his petri dishes 
could kill bacteria, he was on his way to developing the world’s first antibiotic.  
BACK  
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought  
Fleming went on a summer holiday in 1928 and when he came back on 3 September he 
started sorting through his petri dishes containing staphylococcus colonies. Staphylococcus 
bacteria can give you anything from a sore throat, to crusty, weepy rashes, to pneumonia.  
On one of the petri dishes Fleming saw that a piece of penicillin mold had started growing 
and that around the mold the staphylococcus had died. He soon figured out that his “mold 
juice” could kill a range of harmful bacteria.  Fleming’s ability to figure that out changed the 
world and saved millions of lives!

BACK 
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought 
This is what one calls trouble-shooting - tracing and correcting faults through trial and error 
and a lot of thought. Also called “figuring it out”. 
FRONT

BACK 
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought

dawn of civilization the benevolent use of fire, which can be so destructive, probably required 
a lot of thought.  
FRONT

revolution. 
BACK 
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought

meat after a bush fire and discovered that it tasted rather nice. Then he or she thought about 
it and tried it at home… Interestingly enough, cooking meat makes it more digestible and 
therefore unlocks energy more readily. 
FRONT

BACK 
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought

“that”.  
FRONT

encourage good interpersonal relations.  
BACK 
figure out = to understand something or to find the solution to a problem after a lot of 
thought  
Notice the use of the conjunction “that” in this sentence. Figured out that … 
FRONT  
How on earth do you figure out whether a boy likes you or not? 
BACK 
figure out = to understand someone or understand why someone behaves in a certain way

studying his body language. Notice the use of “figure out” with the conjunction “whether”.  
Figure out whether… 
FRONT

because they reveal less of themselves.  
BACK 
figure out = to understand someone or understand why someone behaves in a certain way 
This use of “figure out” focuses on people rather than on things or problems. This is all about 
emotional intelligence and understanding people. Extroverts are usually more sociable than 
introverts because they gain energy from being with others while introverts get energy from 
being by themselves.  

 
 
ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE 
6 
FRONT  
I’ll soon figure that girl out and once I know what makes her tick, I’ll ask her out on a date. 
BACK 
figure out = to understand someone or understand why someone behaves in a certain way

pronouns or proper nouns.  To figure the boy/girl out. To figure him/her out. To figure 
Rebecca or Ronaldo out. 
FRONT  
Once you figure out the horse’s personality, you’ll be able to handle him better.  
BACK 
figure out = to understand someone or understand why someone behaves in a certain way 
In this case the rider does not have to figure out a person out but an animal. Anyone who has 
ever ridden horses knows that, like people, horses have different personalities.   
FRONT 
No-one thought he would pass the difficult chemistry exam but my brother managed to pull 
it off.  
BACK  
pull off = to succeed in doing something difficult 
This student manages to succeed in doing something difficult.  
FRONT  
No-one thought the ultra-marathon runner would finish the race before the cut-off time, 
after he had hurt his knee in a bad fall, but he managed to pull it off.   
BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult 
The phrasal verb “pull off” is often associated with qualities such as daring, courage or 
shrewd intelligence. In this case the runner had the courage and the grit to persist despite his 
injury. Therefore he succeeded. 
FRONT

know-how to save someone from a mountaintop in the middle of a raging storm. 
BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult 
The successful rescue is the result of courage, knowledge and experience.   
FRONT 
Mom, did you see me pull of that soccer move?! Cool, hey!? 
BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult 
Yes, you can pull off a challenging soccer move, a difficult violin piece or a complex karate 
kata if train enough. 
FRONT 
The thieves pulled off a daring heist during the power cut. They managed to steal millions of 
reals. 
BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult

FRONT

BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult

FRONT

ADVANCED PHRASAL VERBS COURSE

BACK 
pull off = to drive a car off a road in order to stop 
One bad thing often leads to another. 
FRONT 
Never drive if you are feeling drowsy. Pull off and rest. 
BACK 
pull off = to succeed at doing something difficult 
Now that is good advice. Sleepy drivers may cause not only their own deaths but also the 
deaths of others.

CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA 
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
1 
CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA  
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
Lesson 10 | Find Out, Figure Out, and Pull Off 
Hi, I’m Sonja Burger. I’m speaking to you from Paarl, a beautiful historic 
town close to Cape town in South Africa. Today, we will look at three 
different phrasal verbs. The first one is to ‘find out’, the second to ‘figure 
out’ and the third one to ‘pull off’. 
Now, ‘find out’ has two different meanings. The first one is to get 
information, either by studying or researching a topic or a question or to 
find information by chance. The second meaning is to be caught doing 
something wrong – to be caught in an offence. Let’s start with the first 
meaning ‘to get information’. The first sample sentence: 
For tomorrow’s lesson, find out who the sculptor of the famous art Deco 
sculpture ‘Christ the Redeemer’ is, the one in Rio. 
So this teacher wants her students to do research to find out information in 
preparation for a lesson. The second sample sentence: 
You all insisting on a family ski trip to Switzerland but has anyone bothered 
to find out how much this trip will cost? 
Asks the father. So his problem is that they haven’t found out, they haven’t 
done the research to get the information to discover the information about 
the cost. So he’s very unhappy about that. 
The third meaning is to get information by chance. 

 
CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA 
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
2 
I found out by chance who my biological mother was when I walked into 
the dentist room one day and there I saw a replica of myself sitting at the 
switchboard. A mirror image. 
So this person was adopted when she was young. But she didn’t seek out to 
find her mother, she didn’t try to find out her mother’s identity; it happened 
by chance. 
It’s important to note that the phrasal verb ‘find out’ is often used with 
conjunctions. Four specific conjunctions: whether, if, about and that. ‘Find 
out whether’, ‘find out if’, ‘find out about’ and fourthly, they ‘found out 
that’. So its whether, if, about and that. When you use the phrasal verb ‘find 
out’ make sure that you pay attention to the correct use of the conjunction. 
And now we look at the second meaning: to be caught in an offence, to be 
found out doing something wrong. And here I’d like to use an example from 
the world of finance: 
Several very wealthy people, who have tried to hide their money illegally in 
offshore companies, were found out when damning papers were leaked 
online. 
So in this case, these very wealthy people tried to hide their money in order 
to evade tax but they were found out. And here it’s important to notice that 
the use, or to notice that the passive voice is normally used in this sense. The 
people were found out; that is passive voice construction. 
Now for our second phrasal verb ‘to figure out.’ We will look at two 
meanings. The first meaning of ‘to figure out’ is to think about a problem or 
a situation until you have found the solution or an answer or until you 

 
CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA 
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
3 
understand what has happened. The second meaning of ‘to figure out’ is to 
understand why a person behaves in a certain way. 
Now to illustrate the first meaning we’re going to look at an example from 
the world of science. 
Once Alexander Fleming had figured out the mould growing in one of his 
petri dishes can kill bacteria, he was on his way to developing the world’s 
first antibiotic. 
Now in 1928, Alexander Fleming went on holiday – summer holiday. And 
when he returned on the 3rd of September he started sorting through his 
petri dishes and he noticed that one of the petri dishes containing a 
staphylococcus colony actually had a bit of mould growing in it and around 
that mould. The solution was clear; the staphylococcus had died. A 
staphylococcus is a nasty bacterium. It can cause anything from a sore throat 
to pneumonia. So Alexander Fleming figured out that this thing growing in 
the petri dish could kill harmful bacteria and his ability to figure that out has 
changed the world and has saved millions of lives. 
The second sample sentence that illustrates this meaning is: 
Management specialists have figured out that the best way to build strong 
work teams is to encourage good interpersonal relationships. 
Notice the use of the conjunction ‘that’ – ‘figure out that’ and use it correctly 
in the future. 
Meaning two, to understand why someone behaves in a specific way. 
Example sentence: 

 
CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA 
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
4 
The young man says “Once I have figured out what makes that girl tick, I’ll 
take her out on a date.” 
Now notice the construction here. You figure someone out. And here you 
would either use a noun, a pronoun or a proper noun. I figure her out. I 
figure him out. I figure the boy or the girl out. I figure Rebecca or Renaldo 
out. And in this case the figuring out is not about figuring out facts of a 
subject but more about emotional intelligence. 
The third phrasal verb is ‘pull off’. Two meanings: to succeed in doing 
something difficult and number two: to drive a car off the road and to come 
to a standstill. Let’s look at the first meaning, to succeed in doing something 
difficult. Example sentence: 
No one thought the ultra-marathon runner would finish the race before the 
cut off time because he had hurt his knee in a bad fall but he managed to 
pull it off. 
So this ultra-marathon runner managed to complete the race successfully 
despite his injury. You will notice that the phrasal verb ‘pull off’ is often used 
with qualities such as courage or daring or shrewd intelligence. In this case, 
the runner succeeded because he had grit and because he could persist. 
And the second meaning is to pull a car off the road. Now in this case it’s not 
to drive off the road as in drive off a road and into a cliff or ditch. It’s a gentle 
getting off the road for a specific reason. Example sentence: 
John, pull off the road immediately; I think we have a flat tire. Can you 
hear that thumping sound? 

 
CURSO DE INGLÊS MAIRO VERGARA 
MONOLINGUAL PHASE 
5 
Yeah, we all know the sickening sound of a flat tire and that would be a good 
reason to pull off. To get off the road. Another reason would be to admire 
the view. 
And that’s all for today’s lesson. So now that you have found out more about 
these phrasal verbs, you’ll be able to figure out the meaning of sentences in 
which they are used and you’ll be able to pull of more complex 
conversations.
